title: Vertical vs horizontal scaling
description: Learn about vertical vs horizontal scaling strategies for distributed systems. Understand when to scale up versus scale out.

data.text: When your application needs to handle more traffic or data, you have two fundamental scaling strategies: **vertical scaling** (scaling up) and **horizontal scaling** (scaling out). Choosing the right approach affects cost, reliability, and your system's ability to grow.
Vertical scaling means adding more resources to a single machine: more CPU cores, more RAM, faster storage, or a faster network connection. You're making the individual server more powerful.

items: Simpler to implement—no changes to application architecture needed
No distributed system complexity (no consensus, no network partitions)
Easier to maintain and debug a single machine
Single point of failure—if the server goes down, everything goes down
Physical limits—you can only add so much CPU/RAM to one machine
Often more expensive per unit of compute capacity

data.title: Limit
data.text: Every machine has a maximum capacity. Eventually, you'll hit hardware limits or cost constraints that make vertical scaling impractical.
Horizontal scaling means adding more machines to your system. You distribute the load across multiple servers, often using a load balancer to route requests.

items: Theoretically unlimited scaling—just add more machines
Better fault tolerance—if one server fails, others continue serving
Often more cost-effective using commodity hardware
Introduces distributed system complexity (consistency, coordination)
Requires application changes to be stateless or share state
More operational complexity (more machines to manage)

data.title: Best Practice
data.text: Design your application to be stateless from the start. This makes horizontal scaling much easier since any server can handle any request.
Start with vertical scaling for simplicity, then transition to horizontal scaling as you grow.

items.title: Choose Vertical Scaling When
items.description: Early-stage applications, simple workloads, databases that are hard to shard, when operational complexity is a concern, or when the cost curve favors upgrading a single machine.

items.title: Choose Horizontal Scaling When
items.description: You need fault tolerance, you've hit hardware limits, you have predictable traffic patterns, your application is designed for distribution, or you need to handle sudden traffic spikes.

items: Most production systems use a hybrid approach—vertical scaling within a horizontal cluster
Databases often start vertical and move to horizontal via sharding when needed
Stateless services are much easier to scale horizontally
Consider read replicas for databases as a form of horizontal scaling
Auto-scaling groups in cloud platforms make horizontal scaling easier
Assuming horizontal scaling solves all performance problems (it doesn't fix bad code)
Scaling horizontally without proper load balancing strategies
Ignoring the cost of distributed system coordination
Failing to make stateless services before attempting horizontal scaling
Not testing failure scenarios when scaling horizontally
